Apple is facing a civil lawsuit in Brazil seeking 300 million reais (approximately US$59 million), alleging that its App Store allows children to download and access casino-style games without meaningful age verification. Details below.

Apple Brazil App Store gambling loophole

Last month, Brazilian officials gave Apple five business days to further explain how it certifies gambling apps, oversees the App Store, and prevents minors from accessing age-restricted content.

This request came three months after the country's National Secretariat for Digital Rights and National Consumer Secretariat first raised queries with Apple and Google over gambling apps allegedly accessible to children.

Days later, a 9to5Mac investigation found around 100 apps disguising gambling platforms as innocuous games or tools to bypass App Store review, with many available for children to download.

According to Tilt (via MacMagazine), Apple is now facing renewed scrutiny in Brazil over minors' access to gambling apps on the App Store.

The report says the Brazilian National Federation of Centers for the Defense of the Rights of Children and Adolescents (Anced), Educafro Brasil, and the Center for Human Rights San Tiago Dantas filed a civil lawsuit on July 30 demanding that Apple establish an effective age verification system for all casino games distributed through the App Store.

According to Estadão, the plaintiffs are also seeking 300 million reais in moral damages.

The lawsuit cites the app "Casino Roulette: Roulettist," which states it is for users 18 and older, but notes that "at no point during the use of the content is age proof, document verification, or facial recognition required."

Tilt notes that the app offers multiple casino games including poker, baccarat, roulette, and slots, with in-app purchases of up to 599.90 reais (approximately US$118).

Although the app is the only one named in the lawsuit, lawyers for Anced claim "there are at least six other apps simulating casinos that, while labeled with an 18+ age rating, are available for minors to download."

In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs are also asking Apple to block any new casino games from being listed without age verification, to continuously monitor existing games, and to submit compliance reports every six months.

If Apple fails to comply within 10 days, the groups are requesting the court impose a daily fine of 500,000 reais (approximately US$98,000).

Responding to Tilt's inquiry, Apple pointed only to parental controls available through Family Sharing, and said it is testing an age verification system in Brazil, planning to "roll it out to all users through a software update in the coming months."
